kushal-pal-singh.reviewDepth: Narrow source-led review under a limited search budget; not independently editorially reviewed; no rubric assigned
kushal-pal-singh.period: DLF IPO 2007 and SEBI proceedings 2011–2020; CCI 2011–2014; Vadra-DLF transaction 2008 and Haryana proceedings 2012–2026
kushal-pal-singh.summary: Singh led DLF, a Gurugram land developer. The record has four separate strands, none of which is a conviction of Singh: (1) a 2014 SEBI order, in force for six months or less before being quashed by a split Tribunal in 2015, about DLF's 2007 IPO disclosures (Singh was a named noticee); (2) a CCI abuse-of-dominance penalty on DLF (company, not Singh); (3) the Vadra-DLF Manesar land sale of 2008 and the Haryana licensing allegations, where the reviewed sources concern DLF, Robert Vadra and the then Haryana government, and report no finding against Singh personally; and (4) reported long-standing Congress ties. Together they show a land developer operating inside a state licensing system, but not a documented personal exchange. No rubric is assigned.
kushal-pal-singh.mechanism: State land licensing and development approvals; Vadra-DLF land sale alleged but not adjudicated against Singh

support.text: SEBI's whole-time member restrained DLF, K. P. Singh and five other executives from the securities market for three years, in an order dated 10 October 2014. The order found, among other things, that DLF had suppressed information about three entities (Sudipti, Felicite, Shalika) in its 2007 IPO documents. It arose from complaints by Kimsuk Krishna Sinha, which the Delhi High Court had directed SEBI to investigate. It records the company and the individuals disputing the charges. No monetary penalty was imposed in this order.
support.source: SEBI order WTM/RKA/IVD-7/117-124/2014, DLF Ltd and others
support.kind: Regulatory finding (later set aside); person named
support.access: PDF full text extracted and read directly

support.text: Tribunal (SAT) in Appeal 331 of 2014 and connected appeals, decision 13 March 2015, bench J. P. Devadhar (Presiding Officer), Jog Singh and A. S. Lamba. The majority held that DLF did not commit fraud on investors and that all relevant material aspects were in the offer documents, and set the order aside. The Presiding Officer dissented, accepting that DLF had used sham share transfers to conceal association with three companies, but found the alleged knowledge of an FIR unsupported and would have reduced the restraint to six months from 10 October 2014.
support.source: SAT judgment, DLF Ltd v SEBI and connected appeals
support.access: PDF text extracted; majority and minority passages read, not the whole 390,000 characters

support.text: Company filing: SEBI appealed under section 15Z; the Supreme Court admitted the appeals on 24 April 2015, granted no stay, and notice issued on interim applications. In October 2015 SEBI sought to restrain a sale of promoter-group preference shares; the Court on 4 November 2015 made no restraining order. DLF states it deposited Rs 630 crore with the Supreme Court in the CCI matter.
support.source: DLF Limited, standalone results note 4, quarter ended June 2020
support.kind: Company disclosure of litigation status; company characterisation
support.access: PDF text extracted and read; company-authored

support.text: Supreme Court order in the Sinha appeals (Civil Appeals 4089-4096 of 2015): disposed of as withdrawn on 25 August 2020, Hrishikesh Roy J. in chamber; the order says it does not affect any other proceedings. Why the appeals were withdrawn is not stated in the summary read.
support.access: Page summary only; full order text not read

support.text: The CCI penalised DLF Rs 630 crore (August 2011) for abusing dominance over apartment buyers after a Belaire owners' complaint; COMPAT upheld the penalty on 19 May 2014. The Supreme Court on 27 August 2014 admitted DLF's appeal and required the amount to be deposited in an interest-bearing deposit. This is a company penalty on contract terms with buyers, not a political-influence finding.
support.access: Both pages read via fetch summary; final outcome in the Supreme Court not found

support.text: CAG report for 2013-14 tabled in the Haryana Assembly on 25 March 2015 criticised the Town and Country Planning Department for not capturing for the exchequer developers' profit above 15 percent when licences were approved and transferred, letting developers earn large profits merely by selling land. It did not name Vadra but named his company Skylight Hospitality, which in 2008 sold a 3.5-acre Manesar plot to DLF for Rs 58 crore. The reporting is Tribune's account of the CAG report; the report itself was not read.
support.access: Article text reviewed; CAG report not fetched

support.text: Chronology as stated by the page: Skylight bought about 3.5 acres for Rs 7.5 crore in 2008, a housing project was permitted days later by the Congress-led Haryana government, and DLF agreed to buy it for Rs 58 crore; the mutation was cancelled by Ashok Khemka in October 2012 and he was transferred; FIR 288 of 1 September 2018 at Kherki Daula named Hooda, Vadra, DLF and Onkareshwar Properties; the ED filed a prosecution complaint in July 2025 alleging Vadra received Rs 58 crore. Allegations only, with the case in trial. The page does not show any charge against Singh personally.
support.kind: Tertiary chronology of allegations and proceedings
support.access: Page text reviewed; tertiary source via fetch tool, cited links not verified

counter.text: SAT's majority found no fraud on investors and set aside the SEBI order; SEBI's appeals were withdrawn in 2020 (the Sinha appeals) with no Supreme Court merits decision found. DLF and the individuals contested every charge before SEBI.

The Tribune records that the Hooda government had earlier given Vadra a clean chit, that the CAG did not name Vadra, and that a Haryana Government statement to the High Court in 2023 reportedly found no rule violated. The 2024 article reports no statement from DLF or Vadra, that the Dhingra commission report was quashed by the High Court for procedural flaws, and that the case is still unresolved.
counter.kind: Absence of outcome and conflicting accounts

counter.text: The Wikipedia biography reports Singh's close ties to the Congress party and Nehru-Gandhi family as a recurring source of controversy, and that Kejriwal alleged corruption in 2011. These are characterisations and allegations, not findings, and the biography is tertiary.
counter.access: Page text reviewed; tertiary source via fetch tool, cited links not verified

kushal-pal-singh.limitations: Not a legal or sanctions opinion. Primary documents: SEBI 2014 order, SAT 2015 judgment, DLF's own filing. Not obtained: the CAG report itself, the Dhingra commission report (not public), the Haryana FIR, the ED complaint, DLF's and Vadra's statements on the land deal, and the final outcome of the CCI appeal. SEBI's later penalty orders were not read. Search capacity was exhausted midway. The Vadra-DLF matter concerns a political family and a developer, not charges against Singh; the benefit to Vadra (Rs 7.5 crore to Rs 58 crore) is a company-level transaction. Not exoneration, not an allegation of personal wrongdoing.

The RBI held directions against the bank, not an order against Kotak personally.

support.text: Kotak Mahindra Bank's filing to the exchanges records that on 24 April 2024 the RBI directed the bank to cease onboarding new customers through online and mobile banking and issuing new credit cards, and that on 12 February 2025, satisfied by remedial measures and an external audit, the RBI lifted the restrictions. The RBI press release the same day describes the 2024 action as under section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act and cites "supervisory concerns" without detail.

counter.access: Page text reviewed; tertiary source via fetch tool, cited links not verified

Wikipedia-based items need verification against orders. Not exoneration.

cyrus-poonawalla.reviewDepth: Narrow source-led review under a limited search budget; not independently editorially reviewed; no rubric assigned
cyrus-poonawalla.summary: Cyrus Poonawalla founded Serum Institute (1966) and is its chairman; his son Adar Poonawalla is CEO and was the public face of Covishield. The only documented state transaction in the reviewed record is company-level: in 2021 the government bought Covishield at a subsidised price and advanced Rs 3,000 crore to Serum for purchases. The reporting is mostly about Adar and the company, describes a strained government relationship, and records no personal exchange by Cyrus. The one personal item is a Parsi-community vaccine-reservation request that Cyrus offered to meet; its outcome is not documented. No rubric.
cyrus-poonawalla.mechanism: Company-level government vaccine procurement and advance; personal exchange not established

support.text: Open magazine (updated 9 July 2021): the government advanced Rs 3,000 crore to Serum in April 2021 and bought doses at a "highly subsidised rate of around US$2 per dose"; the government took over distribution and temporarily banned exports. The piece is a profile of the family. It shows Cyrus only in a 2013 photo with Pranab Mukherjee and describes no party affiliation.
support.source: Open magazine: The Legend of the Poonawallas
support.access: Page text reviewed via fetch summary

support.text: Lists Cyrus Poonawalla as founder and Chairman and MD and Adar as CEO, the company's Covishield programme and the reported August 2020 price estimate of about Rs 225 a dose. Does not cover the 2021 purchases or any political links.

counter.text: The same Open feature says the dose price was roughly a tenth of the global average, relations with the government became strained, the Poonawallas "seem to have unfortunately become scapegoats" for delayed government orders, and the government retook control of procurement in June. Adar describes unprecedented pressure and the financial risk taken on early production. Cyrus said "I am proud of spending the money with which I have enriched myself." Adar supported his father's offer to reserve 60,000 vials for Parsis, which he said was about a day's production.
counter.kind: Alternative explanation, subject responses and limits
counter.access: Page text reviewed via fetch summary

counter.text: Discovery leads on Panama Papers property attachments of relatives and Serum donation channels were not readable and are not used. No relative's or company's case is attributed to Cyrus.

cyrus-poonawalla.limitations: Identity: Serum's 2021 purchase, price and advance concern the company and Adar; Cyrus is chairman and founder. Not verified from primary records: the advance's terms, price per dose, Serum's electoral contributions, Parliament Q&A or PIB statements. The Open article is a single secondary account. Public-health procurement in an emergency has legitimate purposes; no wrongdoing found or alleged by the sources. Not exoneration.
